# Practice job interview questions with Qwen before the real interview

> **In short:** Qwen can play the role of an interviewer, ask you common questions, and give you honest feedback on how your answers come across — clarity, completeness, and confidence. You'll need about 20–30 minutes for one full practice run, and a free account is enough to start. It cannot read your body language or tone, so for video interviews, do at least one round on camera separately.

By the end of this guide, you'll have run a real mock interview with Qwen, gotten concrete feedback on your answers, and saved your best versions for the night before the real thing. This is for anyone with an interview coming up — first job, career change, or just wanting to sound more polished.

## Before you start
- A Qwen account (free sign-up with email or a supported login).
- A device with a browser — a computer is easier for long answers, a phone works too.
- A job title or two in mind that you actually want to practice for.
- About 20–30 minutes for a full session, or 5 minutes for a quick drill.

## Step 1 — Open Qwen and start a fresh chat

Go to Qwen's chat page in your browser, or open the Qwen mobile app if you have it installed. Look for a **"New Chat"** button or a small **"+"** or pencil icon — usually at the top of the sidebar on a computer, or right above the message box on a phone. Click or tap it. A fresh, empty conversation opens with a blank message box at the bottom. Starting fresh matters because leftover context from an earlier chat could push Qwen's questions in the wrong direction. If you don't see a New Chat button, try refreshing the page — sometimes the sidebar hides it on smaller screens.

💬 Example: just type "Hi" first to confirm the chat is responsive, then move to Step 2 to set up the real practice.

You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with no previous messages above it.

## Step 2 — Tell Qwen what role you're practicing for

In the message box, type a short paragraph that gives Qwen the context it needs to ask realistic questions. The more specific you are about the job, the better the questions will be. Mention the job title, the industry, the seniority level, and one or two skills you want to highlight. Press Enter or tap send. Qwen usually replies with a short confirmation like, "Got it — let's practice for a marketing coordinator role." If the reply feels off or skips your details, scroll up, click the **regenerate** button (usually a circular arrow), or retype your setup more simply.

💬 Example: "I have an interview next week for a marketing coordinator role at a mid-size SaaS company. I have 2 years of experience in social media and email campaigns. Please act as the hiring manager and interview me one question at a time. After each answer, give me feedback on clarity, completeness, and confidence, then move to the next question."

You'll know it worked when Qwen replies acknowledging the role and confirms it will go one question at a time.

## Step 3 — Answer the first question like it's real

Read Qwen's question carefully, then answer as if you were sitting in the actual interview. Type your answer in the same box — don't overthink it, don't use perfect essay language, just answer the way you naturally would. The point is to practice, not to write something polished. If you blank out, write "I'm not sure" the way you might say it out loud, then keep going. The more honestly you answer, the more useful Qwen's feedback will be. If the question feels too easy, ask for a harder version before answering — this is normal interview prep, not a sign you're doing it wrong.

💬 Example: if Qwen asks "Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer," you might type something like: "At my old retail job, a customer wanted to return a laptop past the 30-day window. I listened to her frustration, explained the policy, then asked my manager if we could do a store credit as a one-time exception. She agreed, and the customer left happy. I learned that sometimes bending the rules a little keeps a customer for life."

You'll know it worked when you've typed a full, honest answer — anything between 3 and 12 sentences is a typical interview length.

## Step 4 — Ask for specific feedback on your answer

After you finish typing, don't wait for Qwen to move on. Type a follow-up asking it to evaluate what you just said, and be specific about what kind of feedback you want — clarity, completeness, confidence, filler words, structure. Qwen usually gives you a paragraph or two of concrete suggestions, like "your answer is clear but you ramble in the second sentence" or "you named the result but didn't explain your specific role." If you want a number, ask for a score out of 10. If the feedback feels too soft ("great answer, well done!"), push back: ask Qwen to be tougher, since you'd rather hear it now than in a real interview room.

💬 Example: "Before the next question, can you give me feedback on my last answer? Specifically: (1) Was it clear and easy to follow? (2) Did I actually answer what was asked? (3) Did I sound confident or unsure? (4) What is the one thing I should improve? Please be honest — I'd rather hear it from you than from a real interviewer."

You'll know it worked when Qwen responds with specific, actionable feedback — not just a generic compliment, but actual comments about what was strong and what to improve.

## Step 5 — Push yourself with follow-up and pressure questions

Real interviewers rarely stop at one question on a topic — they ask follow-ups like "and what would you do differently?" or "how did your manager react?" So once you've answered and gotten feedback, ask Qwen to dig deeper. Type a message asking for a follow-up, or simply say "ask me a harder version of that one." If you really want to stress-test yourself, ask Qwen to challenge you: "Now push back on my answer as if you don't believe me." This is where most of the real interview prep happens — the first answer is usually fine, but it's the second and third round that separates nervous candidates from confident ones.

💬 Example: "That feedback helps. Now please ask me a follow-up question about the same story — something a real interviewer would press me on. I'll answer, you give me feedback, and then we move on."

You'll know it worked when Qwen asks a sharper, more specific question that builds on what you said — not a brand-new topic.

## Step 6 — Save your best answers for the day before

Once you've practiced for 20–30 minutes and feel you've landed some strong answers, ask Qwen to summarize your session. Then copy your best answers into a notes app, a Google Doc, or even a simple text file on your phone. The night before the interview, re-read your saved answers out loud — this refreshes the words in your mouth so they sound natural, not memorized. If Qwen gave you specific suggestions ("trim the first sentence, end with a number"), apply those edits now and save the cleaner version. Treat the saved file as your personal answer bank — you can reuse and refine it for future interviews.

💬 Example: "Can you give me a summary of the three strongest answers from this session, plus one thing I should remember to improve next time?"

You'll know it worked when you have a short document with your polished answers that you can re-read on the morning of the real interview.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking Qwen to "just give me good answers."** That turns it into a cheat sheet, not practice. You learn by answering yourself and getting feedback, not by copying what Qwen writes.
- **Pasting ten questions into one prompt and answering them all at once.** That's a quiz, not an interview. Real interviews are conversational. Ask Qwen to go one question at a time so you can answer, get feedback, then continue.
- **Stopping after one round of feedback.** The first answer is rarely the best. Ask Qwen to ask the same question again with a follow-up, or to push back, or to make the question harder. Two or three rounds of pressure is where confidence actually builds.
- **Forgetting that Qwen can't read body language or tone.** Qwen evaluates what you *type*, not how you *sound*. If you're prepping for a video interview, do at least one practice round on camera or out loud, separately, to catch the things text can't show.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Even outside job hunting, this same trick works for any high-stakes conversation — a parent-teacher meeting, a price negotiation, a tough email you're about to send. Practice the words before you have to say them.
- **For your business or work:** If you hire people or run interviews yourself, you can flip the script — ask Qwen to generate the five most common weak answers to a question you always ask, so you know what to listen for when you're the one in the chair.
- **If you're just getting started:** This is one of the most useful first things to try with any AI assistant. No technical setup, no cost to begin, and you'll immediately see why "AI as a practice partner" beats "AI as a cheat sheet."

## Try it now

Open Qwen right now and run a single 60-second drill: ask it, "Give me one common interview question for a [your job title] role." Read the question, close the laptop, and answer it out loud in your room. That's it — your first mock interview is done.
